column4: This parable says a secure town received abundant provision from every place, then became ungrateful for Allah’s favors and tasted hunger and fear. It directly reverses the section’s good state and increasing favor when the gift is denied.

After the account in 16:112–113 of a town that denied Allah’s favor, this ayah commands people to eat good provision and be grateful for Allah’s favor. Its own contribution is the direct pairing of received provision with gratitude.

This ayah states that Allah does not change a favor bestowed on a people until they change what is within themselves. It gives a boundary to the section’s account of a favor completed by its giver: the people’s response matters to what follows.

This ayah says Allah favored the believers by sending them a messenger who recites, purifies, and teaches them, after they had been in clear error. It joins favor to the Prophet’s mission and guidance, matching the section’s connection between divine favor and the stages of being guided.

The ayah calls Abraham grateful for Allah’s favors, says Allah chose him, and says He guided him to a straight path. It repeats the section’s specific meeting of favor, gratitude, and guidance in the account of another prophet.

This ayah says Allah will pay believers’ rewards in full and increase them from His bounty. It brings together the section’s two distinct actions—bringing a good to completion and increasing it—in one promise.

This ayah compares worldly life to rain-grown plants that flourish, then become stubble when Allah’s command arrives, though their owners thought they controlled them. The field scene joins the section’s land dictionary sense to its contrast between passing provision and the better lasting outcome.

The believers are told to remember when they were few, oppressed, and afraid of being seized, then Allah gave them shelter, support, and good provision. This staged movement from vulnerability to safety and provision parallels the section’s shelter, guidance, and sufficiency.

Allah says He intends to favor those oppressed in the land, make them leaders, and make them inheritors. It is a specific staged reversal from low status to an enlarged favor, parallel to the section’s account of provision unfolding through stages.

This ayah explains that the wall concealed treasure for two orphan boys and that their Lord wanted them to reach maturity and recover it, as mercy from Him. It makes divine shelter and provision for vulnerable children concrete, with the benefit kept for a later stage.

Addressing the Prophet, this ayah recalls that he did not know the Book or faith before revelation, then says Allah made the revelation a light by which He guides whom He wills. It is a specific parallel to the section’s movement from an earlier state to divine guidance.

This ayah says people should not grieve over what escapes them or exult over what Allah gives, then warns against boastful pride. It directly limits the false reading in 89:15–16 that worldly increase or restriction by itself signifies honor or humiliation.

The section’s dictionary gloss says khayr is what everyone desires. This ayah supplies a specific boundary: people may dislike what is good for them and love what is bad, so immediate desire does not define the good promised in the section.

This ayah says the bad and the good are not equal, even if the abundance of bad things impresses someone. It sets a concrete boundary on reading worldly quantity as the khayr that the section associates with the better outcome.

The section’s dictionary entry gives tending and improving a plot of land as a sense of root ر ب ب. This ayah describes neighboring plots, gardens, crops, and palms watered by the same water yet producing different fruits, making the land sense concrete.

The section’s lexicon defines inʿām as conveying goodness to another. This ayah makes that transfer specific through commands to do good to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, neighbors, and travelers.
The section’s entry for ن ع م includes an increase sense. This ayah says a good deed receives ten like it, a specific example of goodness being multiplied rather than merely returned once.

After asking whether a person has whatever he wishes, this ayah says the Hereafter and the first life belong to Allah. It repeats the section’s paired terms and locates the hoped-for good in the giver who owns both lives.

In the surah that later describes a giver who seeks Allah’s face and becomes satisfied, this ayah says the Hereafter and the first life belong to Allah. It repeats the section’s paired terms and frames both outcomes as belonging to the Lord.

Following the promise in 28:5 to favor the oppressed and make them leaders and heirs, this ayah says Allah would establish them in the land and show Pharaoh and Haman what they feared. Its contribution is the promised favor’s concrete realization.

The section describes the Prophet’s life as moving through distinct states before a future gift brings contentment. This ayah gives a specific promise of ease accompanying hardship, which illuminates the transition from need and vulnerability toward sufficiency.

This ayah repeats the preceding promise that ease accompanies hardship. Its contribution is the second assurance in 94:5–6, reinforcing the section’s movement through successive states toward a good outcome.

Moses says he is in need of whatever good his Lord may send down to him. The next ayah brings a man’s invitation and practical help; this one contributes the expressed need that makes the later provision a specific response.

The section’s dictionary definition for root ر ب ب includes making a good deed complete and sound. This ayah says Allah will set people’s deeds right and forgive them, a concrete parallel to soundness and completion of deeds.

This ayah describes one who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient. It reverses the section’s step in which Allah finds the Prophet in need and makes him sufficient: here apparent self-sufficiency accompanies refusal to give.

This ayah describes someone who seeks the immediate life and hurries toward it, receiving only what Allah wills, before facing Hell. It is a specific boundary to the section’s promise that the later life is better than the first.

This ayah contrasts the previous pursuit of immediate life with the person who seeks the Hereafter and strives for it as a believer, whose effort is appreciated. It gives the better outcome a concrete response and reward.

This ayah distinguishes one who seeks the harvest of the Hereafter, whose harvest Allah increases, from one who seeks the harvest of this world and receives only some of it. It joins the section’s increase detail to its comparison of the two lives.

This ayah compares worldly life to rain-grown vegetation that later dries and scatters. The next ayah, 18:46, names worldly wealth and children as adornment and enduring good deeds as better; 18:45 itself contributes the field’s brief flourishing and decay.
